title: Greenhouse Gas Auditing
desc: Measure, report and reduce greenhouse gas emissions for an organisation using recognised accounting scopes and data checks.
outcomes: Explain scopes 1, 2 and 3 and emission factors.
Collect activity data and calculate emissions.
Produce an inventory report and reduction plan.
task: Build a greenhouse gas inventory for one small organisation (practice case), with boundary, data, factors, hotspot analysis and reduction plan.
condition: A computer, a spreadsheet, public emission factors, two peers and a mentor. A practice dataset may be used.
standard: Boundary is stated; each number has unit and source; calculations reproduce; data quality is rated; plan has measurable targets; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Sustainability officers, finance staff, engineers, consultants in training.
evidence: boundary note, data sheet, inventory, hotspot chart, plan

quiz: What are scope 1, 2 and 3?
Direct, purchased energy, other chain emissions. (Covered in module 1: Why measure emissions. To pass that module: Peer understands.)
What is CO2e?
CO2 equivalent of other gases. (Covered in module 2: Boundaries and scopes. To pass that module: Written and justified.)
Emissions formula?
Activity data x emission factor. (Covered in module 3: Collecting activity data. To pass that module: Sources noted.)
Why record sources?
To audit. (Covered in module 4: Emission factors. To pass that module: Maths correct.)
Name a scope 3 category.
Purchased goods, travel, commuting or waste. (Covered in module 5: Scope 3 estimation. To pass that module: Method stated.)
Double counting?
Counting the same emission twice. (Covered in module 6: Data quality and checks. To pass that module: Issues logged.)
Why local factors?
Grids and fuels differ. (Covered in module 7: Hotspots and targets. To pass that module: Ranked.)
Why state exclusions?
Honesty. (Covered in module 8: Report and verify. To pass that module: Reproducible.)
How rate data quality?
High, medium, low. (Covered in module 8: Report and verify. To pass that module: Reproducible.)
How often update?
Yearly. (Covered in module 8: Report and verify. To pass that module: Reproducible.)

ladder: Why measure emissions

L1: learner can say what CO2e means. Focus module: Why measure emissions (Understand, 3 h). You cannot reduce what you do not count. Key points: Greenhouse gases trap heat; carbon dioxide is the main one. CO2e converts other gases to CO2 equivalent using warming factors. Reporting supports cost saving, customers and rules. Use consistent, recognised methods. Set a baseline year and recalculate if the organisation changes. Link emissions to money and energy savings.

Teach: open with the worked example. Methane has a larger warming effect than CO2 per tonne, so a leaking gas line is expressed as tonnes CO2e. Switching to LED lights saves 2 tonnes CO2e and 20,000 INR per year. Then set the activity: Explain CO2e to a peer. Add a baseline year. Mark against the standard: Peer understands. Check at this level: What are scope 1, 2 and 3? Model answer: Direct, purchased energy, other chain emissions.
Boundaries and scopes

L2: learner knows scopes. Focus module: Boundaries and scopes (Understand, 4 h). Decide what is in and what is out. Key points: Organisational boundary: control or ownership. Scope 1: direct emissions; scope 2: purchased electricity, heat or cooling; scope 3: other chain emissions. Write what is excluded and why. Keep the boundary consistent year to year. Consider whether leased buildings and vehicles are included. Use the same method each year.

Teach: open with the worked example. Company vehicles are scope 1; electricity is scope 2; business flights are scope 3. A company excludes a rented warehouse and records the choice. Then set the activity: Set a boundary for a practice organisation. Record two inclusions and two exclusions. Mark against the standard: Written and justified. Check at this level: What is CO2e? Model answer: CO2 equivalent of other gases.
Collecting activity data

L3: learner can collect data. Focus module: Collecting activity data (Apply, 5 h). Good data comes first. Key points: Bills, meters, fuel logs, travel records. Units must match: litres, kWh, km. Record source and date. Keep invoices. Prefer metered or invoiced data to estimates. Fill gaps with clearly labelled assumptions.

Teach: open with the worked example. Fuel invoices give 1,200 litres of diesel for the year. Missing March fuel data is estimated from February and April and flagged. Then set the activity: Collect data for a case. List data gaps and fixes. Mark against the standard: Sources noted. Check at this level: Emissions formula? Model answer: Activity data x emission factor.
Emission factors

L4: learner can calculate. Focus module: Emission factors (Apply, 5 h). Convert activity to emissions. Key points: Emissions = activity data x factor. Use recent, local factors. Record version and source. Check units. Update emission factors yearly. Show each calculation line by line.

Teach: open with the worked example. 1,200 L x 2.68 kg CO2 per litre = 3,216 kg CO2. A grid factor of 0.82 kg CO2e per kWh applied to 40,000 kWh gives 32,800 kg. Then set the activity: Calculate five lines. Add a factor table with versions. Mark against the standard: Maths correct. Check at this level: Why record sources? Model answer: To audit.
Scope 3 estimation

L5: learner can find hotspots. Focus module: Scope 3 estimation (Analyse, 5 h). The chain is often the largest part. Key points: Purchased goods, travel, commuting, waste. Start with largest categories. Use estimates and say so. Ask suppliers for data. Use spend-based estimates where activity data is not available. Ask the top five suppliers for their data.

Teach: open with the worked example. Travel is 22 per cent of the total; staff commuting 11 per cent. Purchased goods account for 35 per cent of the total using spend factors. Then set the activity: Estimate two categories. Rank scope 3 categories. Mark against the standard: Method stated. Check at this level: Name a scope 3 category. Model answer: Purchased goods, travel, commuting or waste.
Hotspots and targets

L6: learner can lead an inventory. Focus module: Hotspots and targets (Analyse, 4 h). Decide where to act. Key points: Rank sources. Set reduction targets and dates. Cost the actions. Track progress. Prioritise actions by tonnes saved per rupee. Assign owners and dates.

Teach: open with the worked example. Efficient lighting cuts 8 per cent for a payback of 2 years. Fixing refrigerant leaks saves 6 tonnes CO2e for 15,000 INR. Then set the activity: Draw a hotspot chart. Rank five actions. Mark against the standard: Ranked. Check at this level: Double counting? Model answer: Counting the same emission twice.
Report and verify

L7: learner can audit. Focus module: Report and verify (Create, 4 h). Share honestly. Key points: Summary, method, limits. Independent review. Update yearly. Publish what you can. Have a colleague reproduce one result from your sheet. Archive the evidence.

Teach: open with the worked example. The report states excluded sources and the data quality rating. A peer repeats the diesel calculation and gets the same result. Then set the activity: Write the report. Ask a peer to reproduce a number. Mark against the standard: Reproducible. Check at this level: Why local factors? Model answer: Grids and fuels differ.
